_doc: Blueprint for the synthetic dataset. Corpus angles are covered by the ~50 existing submissions; held_out angles NEVER appear in the corpus and are used only for golden 'novel' items, so their novelty is known by construction. See DESIGN.md §3.

corpus_angles.point: The four-day week will reduce burnout and improve employee morale and mental health.
It will help the city recruit and retain staff, since it cannot compete with private-sector salaries.
Residents will face slower response times and more difficulty reaching city offices and staff.
Overtime costs will rise and taxpayers will end up footing the bill.
Ten-hour days are exhausting; tired employees make more mistakes late in the shift.
Ten-hour days clash with childcare and school pickup times for working parents.
How will productivity actually be measured, and can the city's self-reported data be trusted?
One fewer commute day per week cuts emissions, and closing some buildings on the off day saves energy.
It is unfair that private-sector taxpayers fund a perk for public employees that they themselves do not get.
Staggered schedules spread commuting out and reduce rush-hour traffic congestion.
Once granted, the schedule will be very hard to reverse in future union contract negotiations, whatever the data shows.
Downtown lunch spots and shops near city hall will lose weekday foot traffic from city workers.
A generic, low-substance reaction (e.g. 'good idea' or 'waste of money') with no specific argument.

held_out_angles.point: Police, fire and 911 dispatch run 24/7 shifts and cannot compress into four days, so the pilot creates a two-tier workforce inside city government and may hurt morale among excluded staff.

The pilot has no control group; the city should randomly assign some departments to stay on five days (or stagger the rollout) so the quarterly data can show causation rather than a before/after trend.
Longer 10-hour days may be harder for employees with disabilities or chronic illness; the pilot should offer a 5x8 opt-out or flexible alternative to avoid pushing them out.
Starting in January confounds the results with seasonal demand (winter vs. summer permit and park workloads), so a single year of quarterly data could mislead.
Use the pilot as a forcing function to move permits, payments and records requests online, so residents get 24/7 service regardless of office hours.
Neighbouring towns will lose staff to Riverton and may be pushed into copying the policy or raising wages, starting a regional bidding war among municipalities.

items.new_detail: Proposes tracking sick-leave usage and employee assistance program visits per quarter as the concrete burnout metric, compared against the prior three years.
Proposes a public dashboard of permit turnaround times per day of the week so residents can see whether the staggered schedule actually works.
Points out that overtime is concentrated in a few departments (snow removal, water main repair) whose emergencies do not follow any schedule, so the average cost figure will hide the real risk.
